children.text: Santa Ana Parish Church is a coral-stone Gothic church completed around

, known as the "women's church" because sixteen female saints stand on its columns. It faces Molo Plaza, a short jeepney ride from central Iloilo, and in half a day you can see the plaza and Molo Mansion as well.
The official name of Molo Church is Santa Ana Parish Church, and it stands in front of the plaza in Molo District, southwest of Iloilo City. It is about
3km
from the city center. Molo began in
as a separate town where Chinese merchants lived, and was merged into Iloilo City in
. The church still carries the pride of that independent town.
In
Father Pablo Montaño built the first church on this site using the tabique pampango method of clay-and-wood walls. When it fell into disrepair it was replaced by a temporary building in
, plans for a stone church were drawn in
, and the bishop approved them in
. The church you see today was finished around
, and tradition says its coral stone and limestone were set in mortar mixed with egg white. The building is about
long and
wide, and its twin bell towers with red pointed roofs can be seen from anywhere on the plaza.

What makes this church famous is its interior. Sixteen statues of female saints stand on the Corinthian columns on both sides of the central aisle, and there are no male saints, so people call it the "women's church" or the "feminist church." Its style is neo-Gothic, a blend of Gothic and Renaissance, and it counts as one of the rare Gothic-style churches in the Philippines. Female saints looking down on the pews is an arrangement hard to find in other famous churches.
A marker by the entrance from the National Historical Institute says José Rizal visited in
to see the paintings inside. In the final stage of the Second World War the church sheltered local people, but it was badly damaged during the liberation fighting in
and one tower collapsed; Father Manuel Alba and the parishioners restored it after the war. It was declared a national historical landmark in

, and it is still a working parish where Mass is held several times a day. You can see it within half a day alongside other Iloilo sights, which suits travelers interested in church architecture and the old stories of the city.

blocks.title: Twin bell towers and the coral-stone façade

children.text: From the middle of the plaza or in front of the fountain, the gray-white façade and the two red pointed roofs fit into a single frame. Step closer and look one by one at the Corinthian columns on either side of the main door, the rose window and pointed-arch windows above, and the stained-glass window of the Virgin.

Life-size statues of saints such as Lucy, Apollonia, Cecilia, Clare, Martha and Mary Magdalene stand on the columns on both sides of the central aisle. Walk around reading the name plates at their feet, and you will notice the differences in each saint's attributes.

blocks.title: The vaulted ceiling and the crossing dome

children.text: The central ceiling of the cross-shaped plan is a barrel vault packed with plaster ornament, and the dome over the crossing has the four Evangelists painted inside round frames. The murals, painted by local artists and since restored, are worth tipping your head back to enjoy for a while.

The reredos behind the altar is a neo-Gothic structure with soaring spires, and four side altars stand to the left and right. At its center is said to be a figure of St. Anne teaching the young Mary to read scripture.

The plaza in front of the church covers about one hectare and holds a white bandstand surrounded by statues of Greek goddesses, a fountain, and a monument to Maria Clara. After dark, when the lights come on, local families gather and the mood is at its best.
This Yusay-Consing mansion, built in the
, is known for its red tile roof and curved front staircase. The garden and ground-floor shop are open to walk into, so it is a good stop of
10–20 minutes
after visiting the church.

This clear pork broth with pork dumplings and no noodles is the signature dish of Molo. It is sold at many eateries in the Molo district and across the city, and a bowl is cheap enough to enjoy as a snack.
On
July 26

, the feast of the parish patron saint, Mass and a procession are held and the whole area around the plaza fills with people. Time your visit for that week if you want to see a local festival atmosphere very different from the usual quiet of the church.

items.title: Half-day itinerary (afternoon)
items.subtitle: From the church to the plaza and the mansion

children.text: Set out from central Iloilo by jeepney or Grab to Molo (about
15–25 minutes
Look at the church façade first from far down the central path of Molo Plaza, then walk up to the main doors.
Walk along the central aisle and take in the female saints, the ceiling, the crossing dome and the main altar in turn.
Read the historical marker beside the entrance and look closely at the texture of the stone walls below the bell tower.
Look around the plaza bandstand, the Maria Clara monument and the fountain.
Browse the garden and shop of Molo Mansion.
Have an early dinner of pancit Molo, then see the façade once more as the lights come on at dusk.

items.title: Evening itinerary (focused on the night view)

children.text: If you want to avoid the midday heat and see the façade lit up, it is easier to arrive as the sun begins to set.
Arrive at the plaza, rest on a bench, and photograph the façade as the sun goes down.
Look quietly around the inside around evening Mass time. If Mass is in progress, stay near the entrance.
Photograph the illuminated façade and the fountain, and take in Molo Mansion at night as well.
Head back to central Iloilo or Mandurriao district for dinner.
The flight from Manila to Iloilo International Airport (ILO) takes about
1 hour 10 minutes
, with several flights a day. The airport is in Cabatuan, northwest of Iloilo, and the ride into the city takes about
30 minutes to 1 hour
From the airport to the city, a UV Express van costs about
one way, a taxi about
and Grab about

From the city, board a jeepney signed "Molo" or "Arevalo" and get off in front of Molo Plaza. The ride takes about
15–25 minutes

Route numbers can change, so say "Molo Church" to the driver and check before you board.
A taxi or Grab from the city costs around
. Waits can be long at evening rush hour.
A tricycle is handy for getting around inside Molo. Agree on the fare before you get in.
From Bacolod, a fast craft takes about
1 hour
to reach Iloilo's port. From the port, continue to Molo by taxi.
From the Kalibo and Boracay side, the bus or van takes about
5–6 hours
, so staying a night in Iloilo is the realistic plan.
It is about
3km
from the city center to Molo Plaza, about
45 minutes
on foot. It is hot and sunny at midday, so walking is not recommended then.
The dry season from
December
to
May
is the best time for walking.
December to February
is relatively cool in the morning and evening, which makes the plaza pleasant, while in
March to May
daytime highs reach around
and being outdoors at midday is hard. In that season walk the plaza before
or after
, and rest inside the cool church during the hottest hours.
From
June
to
November

is the rainy season, with frequent afternoon showers, but a visit to the church and plaza takes only half a day, so it is perfectly possible in a break between showers. Typhoons mostly affect the area from
August to November
. The plaza has little shade and drains slowly, so water can pool after heavy rain.
Events are also worth considering. During the week of the Feast of St. Anne on
July 26
, Masses and a procession fill the district with crowds. During Holy Week in
April
there are many processions and special Masses, so the times when the interior is restricted increase. Dinagyang, Iloilo's biggest festival, is held around the fourth weekend of
January
, so hotels in the city fill up early.

Molo District itself has few hotels, so most visitors stay in central Iloilo (around Calle Real and the riverside Esplanade) or in the new downtown of Mandurriao and make the trip from there. To stay on the Molo side, there are a few small and mid-sized hotels around M.H. del Pilar Street. Mid-range hotels cost about
a night, and small guesthouses about

Pancit Molo is the food to eat. It is a soup of thin dumpling wrappers filled with a stuffing and floated in pork broth, with no noodles in it, which is the difference from La Paz batchoy. Old neighborhood eateries in Molo and restaurant streets in the city sell a bowl for about
. Molo's famous flavor is so simple that it is really this one soup, so it is better to pair other Iloilo foods such as batchoy and biscocho on the city side.
Dress so that your shoulders and knees are covered. Sleeveless tops may be refused entry, so keep a thin jacket or scarf in your bag.
Some sources say the church is open to visitors Tuesday to Saturday
and
and on Sunday mornings, and some say it is closed on Mondays. Hours change with parish matters, so check with the parish office or the latest notice before you go.
Weekday Masses are at
and
, Saturday evening Mass is at
, and on Sundays there are said to be seven Masses between
. Masses are split between English and Hiligaynon, and the times change on feast days.
The best time to photograph the façade is said to be around dusk,
. Use a wide-angle lens or your phone's 0.5x lens to fit the twin bell towers into one shot.
Turn off the flash when photographing the ceiling and altar, and avoid showing the faces of people at prayer.
Each statue has a name plate below it giving the saint's name. Checking the name along with the attributes makes it fun to work out who is who.
The church, plaza and mansion together take about
1 hour 30 minutes
, so it fits well into an afternoon. Combine it with Jaro Cathedral or a city museum to make a half-day tour.
It costs little, but carry plenty of small change (₱20, ₱50) for jeepney fares. Putting a small amount in the donation box is up to you.

Molo Church is a working parish before it is a sightseeing spot. Weddings, funerals and events can close the inside without notice, so on such days see the exterior and plaza and come back to the interior at another time.
During Mass, do not walk around the pews or take photos. Do not touch the saint statues or altar decorations.
Repair and restoration of the exterior and interior have gone on over the past few years, so some areas may be screened off. Check the latest news just before you visit.
Drone photography may need permission from the parish and the city authorities, so do not fly one without it.
The plaza at night is crowded, so beware of pickpockets. Keep your phone and wallet in front of you.
The plaza has little shade at midday and heatstroke is a risk, so bring water and a hat. In the rainy season, bring an umbrella for sudden showers.
In the week around
July 26
, roads are closed and traffic jams, so travel takes longer.
